description: Connecting capstone work to GitHub's accessibility program and open source at scale.
concepts: GitHub's mission: accelerating human progress through developer collaboration

transcriptText:
[ALEX]
You've reached a really important point. After a capstone, it can be tempting to think, okay, that was the assignment, I did it, time to move on. But what you practiced is bigger than a classroom exercise.

[JAMIE]
Because the habits matter, not just the one project?

[ALEX]
Exactly. In accessibility work, credibility comes from evidence. You practiced naming the user, describing the barrier, proposing a focused change, testing the result or clearly explaining it, and then inviting review. That is real project behavior.

[JAMIE]
I like that, because it makes accessibility feel concrete instead of vague. You're not just saying, this feels inaccessible. You're documenting who is affected, what is happening, what should change, and what happened after you checked.

[ALEX]
Right. And GitHub places that kind of work inside a much larger mission. GitHub describes its mission as accelerating human progress through developer collaboration. Its accessibility program is framed around helping about 1.3 billion people with disabilities benefit from and contribute to that progress.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
That framing is powerful. It says accessibility is not some side quest.

[ALEX]
Yes. It is not a niche afterthought. It shapes who can participate in software, who can become a contributor, and who gets to influence the tools the rest of the world uses.

[JAMIE]
So if a learner listening to this is blind, low vision, neurodivergent, mobility disabled, Deaf, hard of hearing, or has another disability, the message is: you are not outside the story of software development. You are part of it.

[ALEX]
Beautifully said.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
GitHub describes four strategic accessibility priorities, and they connect directly to the kind of work you've been practicing.

[JAMIE]
Let's walk through them one by one.

[ALEX]
First, employees with disabilities. GitHub says accessibility starts at home by supporting employees with disabilities. That includes accessibility training for all GitHub teams, improving internal tools and systems used by employees, supporting employee communities like NeuroCats and AccessCats, and providing accommodations and career growth opportunities.

[JAMIE]
So the idea is that accessibility is not just something a company talks about for customers. It also has to show up in hiring, workplace systems, support, and advancement.

[ALEX]
Exactly. If accessibility is only external, it's incomplete. An organization has to make it possible for disabled people to work there, grow there, and shape decisions from the inside.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Second, developers with disabilities. GitHub says every developer should feel welcome and be able to use GitHub products, documentation, training, support, events, and community spaces.

[JAMIE]
That's broad on purpose, isn't it? Not just the website or one feature.

[ALEX]
Correct. The experience includes product interfaces, docs, learning materials, support channels, events, and community participation. GitHub also lists accessibility as a GitHub Fundamental. That means there are clear expectations for product teams, testing requirements and processes, accountability through GitHub Fundamentals scorecards, and regular audits and compliance tracking.

[JAMIE]
That word fundamental matters. It means accessibility is treated like a core quality expectation, not an optional polish step.

[ALEX]
Yes. And for learners, that should sound familiar. Good accessibility work is planned, tested, reviewed, and tracked.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Third, customers building on GitHub. GitHub shares tools and practices to help customers meet their own accessibility goals.

[JAMIE]
What kinds of tools?

[ALEX]
Examples include a Figma annotation toolkit to support accessible design collaboration, the GitHub Accessibility Scanner action that can be added to a repository's continuous integration checks, guidance for accessibility-focused Copilot custom instructions so AI assistants can help with accessibility audits, and templates and patterns for accessible READMEs, contributing guides, and issue templates.

[JAMIE]
That's a useful list because it spans design, automation, AI-assisted review, and project documentation.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Accessibility is not one tool. It's a workflow. It can begin in design, continue in code review and CI, and show up in contribution docs that make projects more usable and welcoming.

[JAMIE]
And from an accessibility perspective, those templates matter a lot. An accessible README or contributing guide can lower the barrier to entry before someone ever opens an editor.

[ALEX]
Absolutely.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Fourth, open source at scale. GitHub has pledged to help improve accessibility in open source by empowering people with disabilities to contribute to open source projects, increasing free and open source assistive technologies, increasing the accessibility of mainstream open source projects, and providing resources, tools, and guidance to maintainers.

[JAMIE]
That phrase, at scale, is doing a lot of work.

[ALEX]
It is. We're not only talking about one accessible repository. We're talking about habits, tools, and expectations that can spread across thousands of projects.

[JAMIE]
And maintainers are part of that equation too.

[ALEX]
Yes. Contributors matter, and maintainers matter. If maintainers have better guidance, templates, tools, and review practices, accessibility improvements become easier to welcome, evaluate, and sustain.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
I want to connect this back to the learner's capstone, because some people may still think, my project was small.

[ALEX]
A small project can still model excellent practice. Your capstone is an example of accessibility excellence because you named a real user need, described the barrier or opportunity clearly, proposed a focused change, tested the result or explained it carefully, and invited review and feedback.

[JAMIE]
So excellence here is not about flashy scope. It's about disciplined, evidence-based contribution.

[ALEX]
Exactly. This is the same approach GitHub's accessibility program advocates. When you do this in open source after the workshop, you are participating in a larger movement toward accessible software.

[JAMIE]
That's encouraging. You do not have to fix everything everywhere. You can make one well-scoped, well-documented improvement.

[ALEX]
And that kind of improvement is often what real projects need.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Why does all of this matter? Because the connection between your capstone skills and GitHub's accessibility priorities is direct.

[JAMIE]
Let's make that explicit.

[ALEX]
First, your evidence habits scale to thousands of projects. If you know how to identify a barrier, explain it clearly, propose a reasonable fix, and document results, you can bring that method into many repositories.

Second, your contributions help normalize accessibility in open source. Every issue, pull request, review comment, test note, and documentation improvement helps move accessibility from exceptional to expected.

Third, your presence matters. If you are a contributor with a disability, or a contributor with accessibility expertise, you change who has a voice in tool design. You broaden the perspective shaping software.

Fourth, your skills show that accessibility is not separate from engineering. It is engineering.

[JAMIE]
That last point is worth sitting with. Accessibility is not an extra layer added after the real work. It is part of real work.

[ALEX]
Yes. It is part of quality, usability, maintainability, collaboration, and inclusion.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
So where does a learner go next after finishing a workshop like this?

[ALEX]
You've learned the fundamentals, practiced with feedback, and completed a capstone that demonstrates accessibility-focused contribution. From here, reference lessons and advanced materials can help with optional tools and deeper workflows.

But the real work starts after the workshop. The patterns you learned"”finding issues, collaborating with others, reviewing code, building tools, improving documentation"”are the same patterns you will use in real projects where accessibility matters every day.

[JAMIE]
That's a practical message. Not, congratulations, you are done. More like, congratulations, now you know how to participate.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we close, let's include the source-of-truth habit too. If someone wants current facts, where should they check?

[ALEX]
Use official references. GitHub Docs is the general home base for product and workflow documentation. The GitHub Changelog is useful when you need to track updates and evolving features. And GitHub Accessibility is the key source for accessibility commitments, priorities, and related resources.

[JAMIE]
And if someone wants to verify specific areas from what we discussed?

[ALEX]
For GitHub's strategic accessibility priorities, check GitHub Accessibility and GitHub Docs. For the practical picture of what excellence looks like in workflows, GitHub Docs and the GitHub Changelog are useful references. And for the broader why-this-matters and what-comes-next framing, GitHub Docs plus GitHub Accessibility are the right places to confirm current information.

[JAMIE]
I appreciate that. Accessibility work depends on evidence, and that includes checking authoritative sources.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Learn the principles, practice the workflow, and verify the details with current documentation.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
So the takeaway is: your accessibility contribution skills are real, they fit how GitHub thinks about inclusion at scale, and they belong in open source.

[ALEX]
Yes. Your work matters, your perspective matters, and careful, evidence-based contributions can improve software for many more people than you may ever meet.

# GitHub Accessibility and Open Source at Scale

## Why This Chapter Exists

After the capstone, you have done more than complete a classroom exercise. You have practiced the same evidence habits that make accessibility work credible in real projects: naming the user, describing the barrier, proposing a focused change, testing or explaining the result, and inviting review.

GitHub's accessibility program gives that work a larger context. GitHub describes its mission as accelerating human progress through developer collaboration. The accessibility program focuses on enabling about 1.3 billion people with disabilities to benefit from and contribute to that progress.

That framing matters for learners. Accessibility is not a niche afterthought. It is part of who can participate in software, who can become a contributor, and who can shape the tools everyone else uses.

## GitHub's Strategic Accessibility Priorities

GitHub describes four strategic accessibility priorities. The following list summarizes the priorities and how they connect to this workshop.

### Priority 1: Employees with Disabilities

GitHub says accessibility starts at home by supporting employees with disabilities. This includes:

- Requiring accessibility training for all GitHub teams
- Improving internal tools and systems used by employees
- Supporting employee communities such as NeuroCats and AccessCats
- Providing accommodations and career growth opportunities

### Priority 2: Developers with Disabilities

GitHub says every developer should feel welcome and be able to use GitHub products, documentation, training, support, events, and community spaces. Accessibility is listed as a GitHub Fundamental, meaning it has:

- Clear expectations for product teams
- Testing requirements and processes
- Accountability through GitHub Fundamentals scorecards
- Regular audits and compliance tracking

### Priority 3: Customers Building on GitHub

GitHub shares tools and practices to help customers meet their own accessibility goals:

- The Figma annotation toolkit for accessible design collaboration
- The GitHub Accessibility Scanner action you can add to your own repository CI checks
- Guidance for building accessibility-focused Copilot custom instructions so agents help with accessibility audits
- Templates and patterns for accessible README, contributing guides, and issue templates

### Priority 4: Open Source at Scale

GitHub has pledged to help improve accessibility in open source by:

- Empowering people with disabilities to contribute to open source projects
- Increasing free and open source assistive technologies
- Increasing the accessibility of mainstream open source projects
- Providing resources, tools, and guidance to maintainers

## What Excellence Looks Like in Practice

Your capstone work is an example of accessibility excellence. You:

1. Named a real user need
2. Described the barrier or opportunity clearly
3. Proposed a focused change
4. Tested or explained the result
5. Invited review and feedback

This evidence-based approach is exactly what GitHub's accessibility program advocates for. When you do this in open source projects after the workshop, you are contributing to a larger movement toward accessible software.

## Why This Matters

The connection between your capstone skills and GitHub's accessibility priorities is direct:

- Your evidence habits scale to thousands of projects
- Your contributions help normalize accessibility in open source
- Your presence as a contributor with a disability or accessibility expertise changes who has a voice in tool design
- Your skills demonstrate that accessibility is not separate from engineering—it is engineering

## What Comes Next

You have learned the fundamentals, practiced with feedback, and completed a capstone that demonstrates accessibility-focused contribution. The reference episodes that follow offer deeper dives into optional tools and advanced workflows.

But the real work starts after this workshop. The patterns you learned—finding issues, collaborating, reviewing code, building tools—these are the patterns you will use in real projects, where accessibility matters every single day.

## Authoritative Sources

Use these official references when you need the current source of truth for facts in this chapter.

- [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en)
- [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/)
- [GitHub Accessibility](https://accessibility.github.com/)

### Section-Level Source Map

Use this map to verify facts for each major section in this file.

- **GitHub's Strategic Accessibility Priorities:** [GitHub Accessibility](https://accessibility.github.com/), [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en)
- **What Excellence Looks Like in Practice:** [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en), [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/)
- **Why This Matters / What Comes Next:** [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en), [GitHub Accessibility](https://accessibility.github.com/)

Challenge 15 (Discover Accessibility Agents) is browse-first. Learners are not required to fork the accessibility-agents repository to complete it.

[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're working with one of those GitHub features that quietly makes open source collaboration much easier: issue templates.

[JAMIE]
And this is a great one for people who have ever opened a blank issue form and thought, what exactly am I supposed to put here?

[ALEX]
Exactly. An issue template turns that blank box into a guided experience. Instead of guessing what maintainers need, contributors get prompts, structure, and clear required fields. That reduces back-and-forth, improves quality, and helps teams act on issues faster.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just about formatting. It's about making contributions clearer and more usable.

[ALEX]
Yes, and especially in accessibility work. If someone is reporting an accessibility barrier, a vague report can be hard to reproduce. A thoughtful template can ask where the problem occurred, what assistive technology was involved, what the expected behavior was, and how severe the barrier is.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we get into the design challenge, what should learners already have in place?

[ALEX]
A few practical things. First, you should already know how to work with GitHub issues at a basic level. Second, you need a repository where you can create or edit files, usually your fork or your own repo. Third, it really helps to use an editor with YAML syntax highlighting, such as VS Code.

[JAMIE]
And some things are recommended but not strictly required, right?

[ALEX]
Right. Familiarity with GitHub Copilot can help if you want to generate variations, but it's optional. Basic terminal comfort is useful, though you can also use the GitHub web editor or github.dev. And if you already filled out the workshop registration template earlier in this course, that template becomes a learning example now.

[JAMIE]
I like that. You've already used a professional issue template, so now you reverse-engineer it.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Also, there's an administrative note here: this chapter is meant to prepare you for a later workflow using a template-building agent. The advice is to complete the manual template chapter first, then use the automation later.

[JAMIE]
And time-wise?

[ALEX]
Plan roughly two to two and a half hours if you do the exercises and some YAML troubleshooting.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The learning pattern for this challenge is analyze, remix, create, and test.

[JAMIE]
That feels approachable. First understand an existing template, then adapt one, then optionally build another version from scratch, then verify it works.

[ALEX]
That's the idea. The workshop recommendation frames Challenge 14 as design-focused rather than automation-focused. You're producing evidence of understanding, often as an issue comment or a pull request, rather than trying to satisfy a complicated code runtime.

[JAMIE]
Though there is still one small autograded requirement in the challenge template itself.

[ALEX]
Yes. For the assigned challenge issue, the autograder checks that a YAML file exists in the repository
